articles.title_orig: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.title_zh: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.content_orig:
China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air
This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “ flat or falling ” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown .
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “ wasted ” wind and solar fell.
Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.
The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates . This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.
Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.
The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.
Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand .
Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated .
Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust .
This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.
Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “ wasted ”.
The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.
Another key factor is weaker GDP growth . Since reported GDP growth remains within target , however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.
The focus of the economic stimulus announced to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.
These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “ green ” and zero-carbon solutions.

articles.title_orig: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
By SHIVALI BEST, SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR
Published: 14:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EDT, 5 November 2026
Humans have been getting stoned for at least 2,800 years, a new study has revealed.
Scientists from the University of Bern uncovered cannabis seeds in a tomb in Siberia, belonging to high–ranking members of the Scythian society – a horse–riding culture of the Eurasian steppe.
Using radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that the seeds were placed in the grave in the early eighth century BC.
In addition, the scientists found traces of cannabis in human hair collected inside the tomb.
This suggests that the drug had either been inhaled or ingested by one of the tomb's residents.
'The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,' said Dr Gino Caspari, who led the study, published in the journal Science.
Scientists from the University of Bern uncovered cannabis seeds in a tomb in Siberia, belonging to high–ranking members of the Scythian society – a horse–riding culture of the Eurasian steppe
In addition, the scientists found traces of cannabis in human hair collected inside the tomb. This suggests that the drug had either been inhaled or ingested by one of the tomb's residents
While cannabis is one of the most commonly used drugs in the world today, exactly when humans started using it has remained unclear.
Previous studies have shown that cannabis was cultivated in East Asia at least 6,000 years ago, likely initially for its oil–rich seeds.
However, direct evidence of its use has been lacking.
One of the key issues is that plant parts such as flowers, leaves and resins are perishable – meaning they rarely survive.
In their new study, the team explored a tomb in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva.
There, they found about 1,400 cannabis seeds – six of which were in good enough condition to date back around 2,800 years.
'The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,' said Dr Caspari.
However, the seeds alone do no prove that cannabis was consumed by the tomb's residents.
In their new study, the team explored a tomb in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva. There, they found about 1,400 cannabis seeds – six of which were in good enough condition to date back around 2,800 years
The seeds (pictured) alone do no prove that cannabis was consumed by the tomb's residents. Thankfully, the researchers also found human hair in the tomb, which contained 'clear signals' consistent with cannabinol (CBN)
Thankfully, the researchers also found human hair in the tomb, which contained 'clear signals' consistent with cannabinol (CBN).
CBN is produced by the oxidation of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the most important intoxicating compound in cannabis.
In addition, the team detected weak signals that are consistent with THC.
While the discovery within the hair indicates cannabis use, the scientists still don't know how the drug was consumed, or how much of it was taken.
The researchers now hope to analyse the seeds further to understand whether they were specifically selected or cultivated for higher levels of active compounds.
'We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,' says Dr Caspari.
'DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.'
Cannabis is an illegal Class B drug in the UK, meaning possession could result in a five year prison sentence and those who supply the drug face up to 14 years in jail.
However, the drug is widely used for recreational purposes and can make users feel relaxed and happy.
But smoking it can also lead to feelings of panic, anxiety or paranoia.
Scientific studies have shown the drug can alleviate depression, anxiety and stress, but heavy use may worsen depression in the long term by reducing the brain's ability to let go of bad memories.
It can also contribute to mental health problems among people who already have them, or increase users' risk of psychosis or schizophrenia, according to research.
Marijuana can be prescribed for medical uses in more than half of US states, where it is used to combat anxiety, aggression and sleeping problems. Researchers are also looking into whether it could help people with autism,eczema or psoriasis.
Cannabis oil containing the psychoactive chemical THC, which is illegal in the UK, is claimed to have cancer-fighting properties, and one 52 year-old woman from Coventry says she recovered from terminal bowel and stomach cancer by taking the drug.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's Peña resigns as bank collapse triggers political crisis
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's Peña resigns as bank collapse triggers political crisis
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is facing a criminal investigation and impeachment proceedings following the collapse of a major bank he had business links to.
Peña announced his resignation from office earlier on Thursday after Ueno Bank was shut down in the middle of the night due to a solvency crisis, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money and triggering a scandal.
Paraguay’s Attorney General has opened three criminal cases against Peña and other former officials related to the bank crisis.
The lower chamber of Congress has approved his impeachment, accusing him of “serious and systematic dereliction of duty” in connection with his dealings with the bank. The Senate later announced that it would start an impeachment trial.
Peña said he would present himself in the trial and defend himself: “I will do so with arguments and evidence, with respect for the Constitution and the institutions of the Republic,” he said.
Peña submitted his resignation while lawmakers were debating charges brought against him by 35 opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents. The charges proposed “removing from office” the president, who took power in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Soon after he announced he would resign, Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to trigger impeachment proceedings.
Both chambers of Congress then convened a joint session on whether to accept his resignation, but it was adjourned without a decision after several lawmakers walked out in the middle of the vote.
If lawmakers had accepted his resignation, he would have been given immunity and special protections; if they remove him from power, he won’t.
Lawmakers that oppose the president said Peña is still president and must face justice.
His impeachment trial started in the Senate on Thursday night and is expected to continue Friday.
“This guy, Santiago Peña, needs to be jailed. An arrest warrant must be issued … pretrial detention, straight to jail,” Senator Yolanda Paredes told reporters earlier.
Peña’s party, the right-wing Colorado Party, has a majority in both houses of Congress.
The presidential office insisted that Peña would show up to the trial. A spokesperson dismissed rumors that he had fled the country, saying he remains in the capital without specifying his exact whereabouts.
Peña said earlier that he was resigning to give peace of mind to Paraguayans “who entrusted their savings to our financial system.”
“I have made the decision to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our public institutions in mind,” he said in a message posted on social media.
Peña entered office as one of the youngest presidents in Paraguayan history at the age of 44. He served as Minister of Finance from 2015 to 2017 during the presidency of Horacio Cartes and also served as a director of the Central Bank.
He is one of the staunchest allies of US President Donald Trump’s administration and has aligned with Trump’s political priorities, particularly on immigration and security.
In response to the president’s announced resignation, a US State Department spokesperson said the relationship between both countries remains strong: “We remain committed to the enduring relationship between the American and Paraguayan people and look forward to continuing our close cooperation on shared priorities.”
Paraguay’s president became embroiled in the crisis that erupted after the intervention of Ueno Bank, a private institution to which he has been linked and which, during his administration, received millions in funds from public entities, including the Social Security Institute (IPS), which manages the pensions of most of the country’s workers.
CNN contacted the presidency before Peña’s resignation to ask about the allegations against him.
The Central Bank of Paraguay found that Ueno Bank’s solvency ratio — with 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people — had fallen below 50% of the required minimum, “as a result of adjustments made to its financial statements during the regularization process.”
As a result of the resolution or dissolution proceedings, the savings of millions of customers were frozen at the financial institution, which is also known for sponsoring local soccer teams and Paraguay’s national team.
Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández ordered the opening of three cases to investigate “the supervision and resolution of Ueno Bank SA, the placement of public funds in said entity and the actions of authorities from different State institutions.”
Paraguay was shaken by Tuesday’s intervention of Ueno, an institution that, according to authorities, violated limits on loans to related companies.
Paraguay’s Central Bank said Thursday night it would start processing guarantee payments to certain Ueno customers in stages.
Peña announced his resignation after two days of long lines at banks, anxiety and street protests.
The country has been trying to position itself as a regional financial hub by capitalizing on the investment-grade status it attained in recent years, after receiving approval from two of the world’s leading rating agencies.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres, Ivonne Valdés Garay and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Phones 'explode' on Wall Street as 'steamroller' shows up for the AI trade
articles.title_zh: Phones 'explode' on Wall Street as 'steamroller' shows up for the AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Saqib Iqbal Ahmed, Anirban Sen, Nupur Anand and Laura Matthews
NEW YORK, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Phones rang off the hook on Wall Street on Thursday as fear-stricken investors sought guidance from the rapid unraveling of the AI trade.
Spooked retail investors and hedge funds alike dumped stocks, Wall Street's fear gauge spiked ‌and traders rushed to hedge as markets went into a tailspin.
"The steamroller showed up today," said Jim Carroll, senior wealth adviser and portfolio manager at Ballast Rock ‌Private Wealth in Charleston, South Carolina.
The Nasdaq 100 index fell 6.4%, erasing $2.5 trillion in market value on investor fears that the Democratic Party's sweeping midterm victory could stall AI infrastructure expansion, adding more uncertainty to a trade ​that has been on shaky ground for the last several weeks.
"Our phones are exploding with asks for color," John Flood, partner and managing director in the global banking and markets division at Goldman Sachs, said in a note.
A person at another large Wall Street bank said investors were increasingly anxious about the unfolding situation.
The selloff sparked hefty hedging in the equity options market as investors braced for further weakness. Wall Street's most closely watched gauge of anxiety, the Cboe Volatility Index, logged its biggest intraday jump in more than 18 months.
Analysts said much of the selling reflected an unwind of the ‌previous session's rally and of the crowded AI trade that has ⁠driven markets for months.
"There was massive de-risking into midterms and traders were surprised by yesterday's move and got sucked back in," Flood said, adding that hedge funds were selling pockets of the market, like hyperscalers, that they bought the previous day.
Options activity was a mix of traders looking for ⁠fresh protection in semiconductors and AI names alongside those taking profits on existing hedges, said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivative strategy at Susquehanna Financial.
The VIX, an options-based indicator that reflects demand for protection against drops in the stock market, jumped 11.75 points to an eight-month high of 28.36, a day after markets rallied following Democrats' victory.
The index closed at 28.18, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% as investors ​fretted ​that a changing of the guard in Washington might slow the pace of AI infrastructure development.
The selloff was in ​sharp contrast to the upbeat market reaction the day before, when ‌investors largely brushed aside the perceived threat to the AI trade from the election results.
"Yesterday there was the perception that no one needed protection and now it's 'Oh my god, we need it'," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.
Analysts attributed some of the decline to investors looking to get ahead of anticipated selling from strategies that react to market volatility.
Leveraged and inverse exchange-traded funds, along with some systematic strategies, typically rebalance near the market close. They also tend to respond as markets grow more volatile, which can amplify market moves.
Leveraged ETFs were expected to sell about $47 billion of stocks into the close as they rebalance, according to an intraday note from Nomura. That would make it the second-largest amount in Nomura's data going back to ‌July 2006, with most of it coming from tech and AI-focused funds.
HEDGE FUND, RETAIL REACTION
Hedge funds were ​also feeling the pain.
According to a Goldman Sachs prime brokerage report sent to clients on November 5, large ​multi-strategy hedge funds were down "significantly" due to outsized exposure to large AI stocks. Technology, ​media and telecommunications-focused funds were down 2.6% from a year ago, Goldman said.
Much now depends on whether investors' attitude toward the AI trade undergoes ‌a lasting change, analysts said.
"If the re-evaluation of the AI investment theme ​is secular and not just a trading type ​of rebalance, that's problematic," said Sosnick.
Retail selling added to market pressure. About one hour before the close, they were on track for their largest day of selling across single stocks since the COVID-related crash, said Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, in an intraday note.
"On a typical sell-off, retail buy the dip. Today, that bid ​has effectively disappeared from individual names," Patel said.
In the options market, ‌the stock market drop boosted demand for hedges, with put premiums — the prices investors pay to buy contracts that protect against a market drop — running at ​about two times what is typical across index products, according to options analytics service Mercury Alerts.
(Reporting by Saqib Iqbal Ahmed; Additional reporting by Laura Matthews, Anirban Sen, ​Nupur Anand, Suzanne McGee; editing by Megan Davies, Kirsten Donovan, Nia Williams and David Gaffen)

articles.title_orig: Stocks Erase Post-Midterm Elections Rally, Dragged Down by Tech
articles.title_zh: Stocks Erase Post-Midterm Elections Rally, Dragged Down by Tech
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 4.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.5%, with the tech-heavy index closing in correction territory.
The Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) fell 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value.
The PHLX Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) plummeted 12% as Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip names sank. Wall Street unloaded this year's AI winners , while large-cap tech stocks saw the worst day since the COVID-19 pandemic sell-off.
Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.
Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil ( BZ=F ) prices traded around $98 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude ( CL=F ) stood at $90 per barrel.
A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.
On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy ( DUK ), Airbnb ( ABNB ), and Lumentum ( LITE ), among others, report results.
Stocks plunged on Thursday amid carnage in the AI trade on Wall Street.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) plunged 4.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 5.5%, closing in correction territory.
Chip stocks took the brunt of the beating, with severe losses for Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ), among others. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank 12%.
Institutional investors dumped the top performers of 2026 to lock in gains. Retail traders followed suit, unloading $358 million of equities in their biggest selling day since 2020.
Meanwhile, regulatory concerns weighed on AI data center build-out stocks. SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) also plummeted over fears of regulatory hurdles following Democrats' congressional victory.
Retail investors are dumping US stocks at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $358 million in individual US stocks on Thursday as of 2:58 p.m. ET, according to Vanda Research, putting them on track for their biggest single-day net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
The selling marks a departure from retail investors' tendency to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued purchasing leveraged exchange-traded funds such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.
The AI trade's marquee stocks got clobbered on Thursday, sparking warnings on Wall Street of an institutional shakeout as investors move to lock in gains.
"They're shooting the generals," wrote Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott on Thursday.
The unwinding of the 2026 popular thematic stocks has been "wildly acute" for more than a month, the strategist noted. The primary catalyst isn't about a sudden deterioration in fundamentals, but a frantic dash by hedge funds to lock in their profits before the end of the year.
"Single-name stock moves are absolutely BONKERS," wrote McElligott. "The Momentum/High Sharpe unwind has been so substantial that we are approaching the dreaded 'Round Trip' levels in some trades."
The carnage has hit semiconductor and hardware stocks particularly hard. Shares of Lam Research ( LRCX ) are down 36% over the past month. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) has shed 30% over the past month, while AMD ( AMD ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are also down 22% and 15%, respectively, over the same period.
Goldman Sachs ( GS ) promoted 109 employees to its coveted partnership on Thursday, its largest class since 2010, as the Wall Street giant elevated record numbers of asset managers and engineers to its senior ranks.
The new class is nearly 15% larger than in 2024 when Goldman named 95 partners, according to a statement from the bank.
Of the 109 new partners, 60 work in Goldman's investment banking and trading division, while 33 are in Asset & Wealth Management. The firm also promoted 13 engineers.
In a departure from previous years, a Goldman executive declined to disclose the gender and racial makeup of the new class, citing changes in the legal environment. The executive added that with the latest round of promotions, the firm has more than 100 female partners.
Partnership status at Goldman is considered highly exclusive. The firm promotes new partners every two years. The promotion comes with higher compensation and additional financial benefits, including opportunities to invest in the firm's private funds.
Once promotions take effect in January, Goldman will have a little over 500 partners, an executive said, amounting to roughly 1% of Goldman's workforce.
It's a bad day for the stock market.
Major indexes are falling Thursday, with technology stocks leading the sell-off and semiconductor shares among the biggest decliners.
But one rough session doesn't necessarily amount to what investors deem a correction.
A correction generally refers to a decline of at least 10% from a recent high in a stock, index, or other asset. It is typically seen as a meaningful pullback, but one that stops short of a bear market, which is commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more.
That distinction matters after Wednesday's sharp rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) and the narrower Nasdaq-100 are each on pace to close Thursday in correction territory, as is the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ).
Meanwhile, the Dow and S&P 500 (down 3% and 4% from yesterday) aren't close to correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) just fell below its 200-day moving average, according to AlphaSpace data (see chart below).
Several individual names, such as Nvidia ( NVDA ), also broke through their 200-day averages, a technical indicator that tracks a stock's long-term trend.
"I think this has been brewing for quite some so much time because there have been so many investors poking at this perceived AI bubble, almost hoping it's going to burst, Hennion & Walsh chief investment officer Kevin Mahn told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
"So this type of volatility shouldn't necessarily come as a surprise to anybody … but there's going to be more choppiness ahead," Mahn added.
As AMD ( AMD ) stock falls 15% amid a chip stock rout on Thursday, the company's CEO Lisa Su told Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi she doesn't see the AI chips demand slowing down anytime soon.
"I think the market can sometimes be a little bit short-sighted. It is what it is," Su said on Sozzi Unleashed .

articles.title_orig: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.title_zh: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in AI development.
Following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI, shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index closed down by more than 5.5% to lose an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
Democrats in races across the US  campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.

You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.

articles.title_orig: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
articles.title_zh: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
articles.content_orig:
Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.
Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.
The new MDR-3R (note the slightly different name) headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions.
New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector.
“The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize,” Sony’s announcement says.
For better or worse, the new headphones also use “the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original,” per Sony. Audiophiles will prefer something more advanced, perhaps with additional acoustic features. A review of the new headphones from Gizmodo says that the MDR-3R headphones “hold their own,” have “bright and clear” mids and highs, and good stereo separation. However, we don’t expect strong bass.
Unlike their predecessor, the MDR-3R has an in-line remote control and an integrated microphone. Without noise-canceling, though, the microphone isn’t ideal for calls in noisy environments.
But nostalgic gear isn’t about having top-of-the-line capabilities; it’s about showing off your love of old-school tech while enjoying familiar technologies that have reliably served their functions for years.
The MDR-3R may also capitalize on surging renewed interest in wired headphones and even physical media and Walkmans. Today’s Walkmans aren’t cassette players, of course, but are Android-powered , touchscreen media players.
The headphones are available for $60.

articles.title_orig: Why the midterm blue wave just triggered a red Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Why the midterm blue wave just triggered a red Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Tech firms tumbled on Thursday as investors contemplated the outlook for the AI boom after Democrats swept the US midterms, partly on the back of growing anger over the rapid building of data centres across the country.
However, broader markets mostly rallied and oil plunged after President Donald Trump's Republicans were dealt a historic defeat that was blamed on high prices, tariffs and the Iran war.
The result stoked hopes he will look to wind down the Middle East conflict, which would help temper inflation and even soften his stance on trade.
But AI-linked firms came under the cosh amid fears for planned data centre construction projects as well as renewed scrutiny from newly installed Democrats on Capitol Hill.
The sector had already been in the crosshairs of investors owing to questions about the vast sums pumped into new facilities, R&D and chip development, and when any companies would see a profit.
Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets said the vote was accelerating a reassessment of AI that was already under way.
"A Democratic Congress introduces another layer of uncertainty: regulatory scrutiny," she wrote, adding that the three main risks were more oversight, data centre restrictions and capital spending uncertainty.
"The congressional scrutiny could accelerate demands for AI safety standards, independent model evaluations and greater accountability for data centre developers," she added.
However, she also said: "This is not the same as an outright anti-AI policy agenda. AI is strategically important for US competitiveness, particularly against China, and there remains considerable bipartisan interest in maintaining American leadership."
Chip firms were hammered in Asia, with South Korea's SK hynix off more than 7% and Samsung 5.5% down.
Tokyo-listed Kioxia dived more than 13% and Advantest tanked 14.7%, while Tokyo Electron lost more than 9% and SoftBank 6.8%.
US Nasdaq futures fell more than 1%.
Broader markets performed better as investors rotated into other sectors including finance, auto, mining and manufacturing names.
Seoul, the poster child of the AI-led surge in the first half of the year, shed more than 5%, while Taipei lost more than 3%. Tokyo gave up 1.8%.
But there were healthy gains in Hong Kong, helped by hopes for an easing of trade tensions between the US and China, with tech titans including Alibaba, JD.com and Tencent leading the way amid a shift into beaten-down regional stocks.
Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai, Jakarta and Manila also advanced.
London, Paris and Frankfurt opened higher to extend Wednesday's spike.
Oil held losses after diving more than 8% Wednesday on the US result amid optimism Trump will seek a deal to end the Iran war, which has been a key driver of the inflation spike that has hammered US consumers.
Hopes received a boost when US Vice President JD Vance said in a social media post that the Republican defeat was due to the unpopularity of the eight-month-old conflict.
The drop in crude prices - both main contracts are now below $100 for the first time since the start of October - has also tempered inflation worries and, in turn, Treasury yields, which dipped again Thursday.
The lower cost of borrowing has also been helped by the prospect that gridlock on Capitol Hill would lead to less spending.
That also weighed on the dollar, which held losses against its peers in Asian trade.

articles.title_orig: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.title_zh: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
articles.content_orig:
Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing.
The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.
The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students. If they don’t want any AI, they can leave it all off. Essentially, Google is giving schools that want to completely block AI the ability to go all the way, even removing search from student accounts.
A Google spokesperson tells Ars that the company has not made any changes to the new policy it announced this week. However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do. There are still reasons to dislike Google’s approach, but here’s how the company explains the process for schools:
As things currently stand, schools can block the Gemini app, but the AI tools in search (AI Overviews and AI Mode) are still present and offer many of the same intellectual shortcuts. When schools choose which AI features to use under this new system, search will be one of the options. Schools can leave search off if they want, but opting in will require them to choose the standard AI features or the new Guided Learning version, which won’t give away answers as readily (or so Google claims).
Schools are gaining the ability to block Google’s AI tools, even those in search, while keeping other Google apps. Notably, the company’s new approach to “responsible AI for learning” does not include the ability to use search without AI. So schools get more control, even if they don’t get the AI-free search everyone seems to want.
Many will argue that Google should let schools access web search without chatbots. However, that’s just not something Google wants to support at any level because it sees AI as the future of search. While other search engines have settings to turn off AI tools, Google steadfastly refuses to create such a toggle (and those no-AI tricks you rely on may not work forever). Ultimately, this is the core problem not just for education customers, but for everyone who wants to limit their exposure to AI while using Google.
This clarification does not change the calculus for educators who want to allow students to search the Internet without AI tools. Google won’t offer that, and switching to another provider is easier said than done. Google still has by far the most expansive index of the Internet, leaving alternatives with numerous gaps. That may change in the near future, though. As a result of Google’s loss in the DOJ’s search antitrust case , it will have to provide competitors limited access to its index of the web. This could give other provides a chance to improve and offer a more viable alternative to Google.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market on Nov. 5, 2026: Nasdaq falls more than 5% in worst selloff since tariff tantrum; Dow slumps more than 1,800 points as selling spreads beyond tech
articles.title_zh: Stock Market on Nov. 5, 2026: Nasdaq falls more than 5% in worst selloff since tariff tantrum; Dow slumps more than 1,800 points as selling spreads beyond tech
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Donald Trump's celebration of Wall Street's highs aged rather poorly. Less than 24 hours after boasting about Americans' retirement accounts going "through the roof," the S&P 500 plunged as much as 3.8% Thursday, bringing emergency trading halts into the conversation.
The selloff prompted traders to monitor the market's circuit-breaker thresholds, which can temporarily shut down trading across U.S. stock exchanges when losses become too severe. The S&P 500 would need to fall another 3.2 percentage points from its decline to trigger the first emergency halt.
The timing is particularly awkward for Trump, who has repeatedly pointed to stock market performance as evidence of his administration's economic success.
"Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof," Trump wrote Wednesday on his Truth Social account. He closed the message with "Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP."
Wall Street had rallied Wednesday following the Democratic Party's sweeping midterm election victories. The S&P 500 gained 1.6%, its strongest daily performance in three months, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 1,500 points to 53.361 points.
Thursday's losses erase that rally in a single session, with technology stocks taking the biggest beating.
The U.S. stock market has three emergency thresholds designed to slow panic selling. These mechanisms, known as circuit breakers, automatically suspend trading when the S&P 500 falls by a specified percentage from its previous closing price.
The first threshold is a 7% decline, corresponding to an S&P 500 level of 7,150.41 points for Thursday's session. Reaching that level before 3:25 p.m. ET would trigger a 15-minute halt across US equity markets.
The circuit breaker level is located in the following chart's blue line
A 13% decline, or 6,689.09 points, would trigger another 15-minute suspension. The most severe threshold comes at 20%, or 6,150.89 points, which would shut down trading for the remainder of the day.
Under the New York Stock Exchange's rules, the first two circuit breakers stop applying at 3:25 p.m. ET, while the 20% threshold remains active throughout the session.
The rules apply to the entire U.S. equity market, not just stocks included in the S&P 500. A market-wide halt would also suspend trading in companies listed on the Nasdaq and other US exchanges.
The technology sector was particularly hard hit as investors continued digesting the consequences of Tuesday's election results. At around 11 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite had fallen nearly 5%, while the S&P 500 was down 3.2%.
Nvidia lost more than 6%, while the broader semiconductor index plunged nearly 11%. Companies involved in building AI infrastructure were also under pressure as investors worried that Democratic victories could bring stricter oversight of data-center construction.
"We suspect there is going to be some scrutiny on this aggressive AI buildout," Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank, told Reuters .
The selloff also spilled into cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin fell below $76,000, wiping out its post-election recovery as approximately $428 million in leveraged crypto long positions were liquidated within an hour, as Decrypt reported earlier today.
Stocks also faced pressure from persistent inflation concerns and uncertainty over the Federal Reserve's next interest-rate decision. Investors are awaiting Friday's October employment report, which could provide further clues about the direction of monetary policy.
Despite Thursday's sharp losses, the S&P 500 had not reached its first market-wide circuit breaker at the time of this report.

articles.title_zh: As Nvidia’s stock enters a bear market, bargain hunters see a golden buying opportunity
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.
Thursday did a lot of the damage . Nvidia closed down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a single session and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. It was the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.
Nvidia has plenty of company.
AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) suffered steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) fell more than 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) had its worst day since March 2020 and is now more than a third below its June record. Sandisk ( SNDK ) dropped 22%.
Nvidia itself is now about 24% below its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .
The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.
Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.
The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.
That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.
For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.
"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

In its fiscal second-quarter report, NVIDIA posted revenue of $96.22 billion, up 105.85%. Consensus was $92.07 billion. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $2.22 against estimates of $2.09. Data Center revenue rose 117% to $89.02 billion. For the current quarter, the company guided to $108.0 billion ±2%.
Management's early outlook calls for about 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, and it says supply is the limit. CEO Jensen Huang said, "The unconstrained number would be a lot higher." Cramer made a related point on August 28: NVIDIA "always looks expensive" on forward estimates, and then "it so far trumps those estimates" that the old multiple looks low in hindsight.
On X, Cramer wrote: "If the cheapest asset is your stock, you should buy it. Nvidia can buy and reload... or they can let it go down." NVIDIA had $99 billion left on its repurchase authorization at the end of the second quarter. During that quarter, it returned $26 billion, with $20 billion of that in buybacks. Year to date, it has returned 60% of free cash flow, above its 50% or more target. Cramer has pushed this idea for weeks. On September 1, he called the stock "radically cheap."
Several concerns explain the low multiple:
Margins: Gross margin was 75% last quarter. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter as memory costs rise.
Financing: NVIDIA has put nearly $50 billion into frontier AI labs. Huang replied to critics who call this circular financing: "We see it differently."
Balance sheet: Supply commitments have risen to $279 billion. Days sales outstanding, the average time it takes to collect payment, extended to 60 days from 45.
China: The outlook assumes no China data center compute revenue.
On valuation, the numbers back him. The stock trades at about 20x this year's earnings and 12x next year's, against a long-run average of 30x. That is a decade low by any reasonable reading.
A low multiple also shows investors doubt that growth will last. Fiscal 2028 EPS estimates range from $12.8484 to $18.746, a wide spread. NVIDIA's next earnings report is the test. articles.title_orig: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles broke out in Nantes and authorities arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by an estimated 575,000 people – remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike was organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors were impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
Our live coverage of the protests in France has ended for the day. Read more on the topic here
At least 448 people have been detained during the nationwide protests in France, the country’s Interior Ministry said, though that is a fraction of the estimated 575,000 who took part.
The ministry revised down its count of protesters, from the 600,000 it reported earlier today .
There were about 65,000 protesters in Paris alone, the ministry said.
The marches across the country were largely peaceful and proceeded without major incidents, the ministry said. There were some clashes between police and “groups of radical and far-left activists” in places like Rennes, Nantes, Lyon and Marseille, it said.
Firefighters responded to 86 fires, including one at a school common room that was destroyed in Toulouse, it said. An effigy of a police riot officer was set on fire in Strasbourg.
Hundreds of thousands of people are protesting across France today, but it’s a movement that grew out of protests that happened two months ago.
In September, students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs went on strike, demanding more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
The movement has since swelled into a collective cry of anger, bringing together groups with different grievances, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
No longer confined to students, the movement has drawn in trade unions and yellow vest protesters, who are voicing frustrations over the cost of living and calling for French President Emmanuel Macron to go. The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions.
With so many causes now fueling the protests, the anger is unlikely to subside anytime soon.
And with France heading into a deeply divisive presidential election in April , the stakes are only getting higher.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed at the end of October that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
The skyrocketing cost of living in France is one of the factors driving this wave of protests as anxieties around low wages, high prices and the state of public services explode onto the streets.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. So why are fuel costs falling?
articles.title_zh: Gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. So why are fuel costs falling?
articles.content_orig:
Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.
Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving, he said.
Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was largely due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Other factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.
The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.
Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual.
"Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. "A more normal markup would be 40 cents a gallon, and that means that even if futures prices and physical markets hang around present levels, we should see lower pump prices for the foreseeable future."
The Trump administration has used various tools to ease gas prices. That includes expanding access to tax-free red-dyed diesel , opening the door to Russian diesel imports , and waiving what's known as the Jones Act , a federal statute that requires goods shipped between U.S. ports to be moved on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed.

articles.title_orig: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.
The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.
Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.
The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.
Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

Anthropic is using artificial intelligence to accelerate development of its own AI models, even as CEO Dario Amodei has warned about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly, according to research reported Thursday by The Associated Press.
Researchers at the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) found that Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, is improving its AI systems on certain measurable tasks at roughly twice its previous pace.
The findings, based on an 11-week review of internal data and employee interviews, suggest Anthropic's growing reliance on AI to help build more advanced models is driving much of the acceleration, rather than increases in computing power alone.
The rapid progress highlights a challenge facing AI developers: increasingly capable systems could help create their successors faster than companies can evaluate potential safety risks.
Researchers cautioned that their estimates carry substantial uncertainty and may not apply to more complex tasks.
Artificial intelligence stocks suffered steep losses Thursday, pushing the Nasdaq into correction territory as investors worried that tougher restrictions on data center construction could threaten the industry's rapid expansion.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.4% in late trading, putting it more than 10% below its recent record, while the S&P 500 dropped 4.3% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1,844 points, according to CNBC.
AI chipmakers Nvidia and Broadcom each tumbled roughly 9%, while Oracle lost 7% and cloud computing company CoreWeave declined 11%.
The selloff followed sweeping Democratic midterm victories that raised concerns about potential limits on new data centers, adding uncertainty to the billions of dollars technology companies are investing in AI infrastructure.
A North Carolina man is suing OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT helped his estranged wife plan to poison him and conceal her actions, according to a lawsuit reported by USA TODAY.
James Gates alleges the chatbot provided his wife, Cheryl Gates, with information about dangerous substances and avoiding detection. He says he became seriously ill in July 2025 and later discovered handwritten notes outlining a poisoning plan.
Investigators obtained ChatGPT conversations that Gates' attorneys argue show the chatbot helped develop the alleged plot.
Cheryl Gates was indicted in October 2025, but prosecutors dropped all charges in April, citing insufficient evidence that an attempted poisoning occurred. She faces no remaining criminal charges.
OpenAI told USA TODAY it banned the user involved and provided information to law enforcement during the investigation.
Google is turning to Hollywood star Henry Cavill to showcase how artificial intelligence can help create video games, launching a celebrity-driven experiment that also raises money for men's health, according to GamesRadar+.
The former Superman actor helped develop a retro-style game called Mustache Protocol using Google's AI tools, demonstrating how the technology can turn ideas and prompts into playable experiences without traditional game development.
The project doubles as a fundraising campaign for Movember, with Google pledging $11 for each completed playthrough, up to $500,000.
The game also draws on a memorable moment in Cavill's Hollywood career: the digital removal of his mustache during reshoots for the 2017 superhero film "Justice League."
The promotion comes as technology companies increasingly market AI tools as a way for people without specialized programming experience to create software, games and other digital content.
A sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks sent Wall Street tumbling Thursday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq toward correction territory as investors grew increasingly concerned about soaring AI spending and potential restrictions on data center construction.
The Nasdaq plunged nearly 5%, while the S&P 500 sank 3.2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed more than 1,000 points in late-morning trading.
The selloff was fueled in part by concerns that sweeping Democratic victories in Tuesday's midterm elections could lead to tougher restrictions on new AI data centers, threatening the rapid infrastructure expansion powering the technology boom.
Chipmakers were among the hardest hit, with Nvidia falling 6.3% and Advanced Micro Devices tumbling 13.1%. AI cloud computing company CoreWeave dropped 10%.
The Nasdaq fell more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record closing high, putting the index on track to confirm its second correction of the year.
Investors have also grown increasingly skeptical about whether the billions of dollars technology companies are pouring into AI chips, data centers and other infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
Meta is welcoming rival OpenAI's pledge to cover the energy costs associated with its massive AI data centers — while pointing out that the Facebook parent company says it made a similar commitment earlier this year.
"This is a good thing," Meta communications official Andy Stone wrote Thursday on X in response to OpenAI's announcement.
"We're glad OpenAI is joining Meta in a long-ago commitment Meta made to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities," Stone added.
Meta publicly outlined its commitments in March , pledging to cover the energy and water costs associated with its data centers, invest in new and upgraded power grid infrastructure, and help ensure those expenses are not passed on to local consumers.
The remarks come as OpenAI seeks to ease concerns about the impact of its expanding data center footprint on electricity bills and local communities.
OpenAI also announced new transparency measures Thursday, including a commitment to stop using non-disclosure agreements with public officials during negotiations over future data center sites and to provide residents with information about construction plans and potential traffic, noise and lighting disruptions.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is pushing back against a vision of the future outlined by rival Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, warning that humans must never surrender control to superintelligent artificial intelligence .
"People should always be in control of the future," Altman wrote in a post on X Tuesday evening.
Altman said OpenAI opposes the idea of humans being relegated to activities that "AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans," borrowing language directly from a 2024 essay by Amodei titled " Machines of Loving Grace ."
In the essay, Amodei explored how economies might function if AI systems eventually became capable of performing most human work. One possibility he raised involved AI-run economies distributing resources to people based on activities the systems deemed worth rewarding.
Amodei presented the arrangement as one of several speculative possibilities, acknowledging that such systems could create serious problems and potentially dystopian outcomes.
Altman did not mention Amodei by name, but his use of the identical phrase points to the Anthropic chief's earlier writing.
"People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress," Altman added.
Meta is making a new play in the artificial intelligence arms race, acquiring a startup that allows software developers to deploy and manage multiple AI coding agents at the same time.
The Facebook and Instagram parent company has acquired Conductor, a startup founded in 2024 that developed a platform for coordinating AI agents working on software projects simultaneously, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.

The IRS has released the 2027 standard deduction amounts you'll use for your 2027 tax return — and they're higher than ever.
The federal tax agency adjusts these amounts for each filing status every year. Since these adjustments are based on inflation, the standard deduction is higher for 2027 than in recent years.
Knowing the standard deduction for your status can help you determine whether you should plan to itemize or claim the standard deduction next year.

Taxpayers age 65 and older, as well as those who are blind, can claim an additional standard deduction . For 2027, that additional amount is $1,700 ($2,100 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse).
Those eligible can add the extra standard deduction to the regular amount for their filing status. A single taxpayer 65 or older (or who is blind) can claim a total standard deduction of $18,700 on their 2027 federal tax return.
Additionally, as Kiplinger has reported, the 2025 Trump tax bill introduced a new bonus standard deduction of $6,000 for those age 65 and older.
This can be added to the 2027 standard deduction for each eligible individual and can be claimed by those who itemize.
However, the "bonus" amount is temporary and phases out for incomes above certain thresholds.
Your standard deduction amount might differ if you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal tax return.
The 2027 standard deduction for dependents is limited to either $1,400 or the sum of $500 and the dependent's earned income, whichever is greater.
Note: The standard deduction for dependents cannot exceed the regular standard deduction for your filing status, even if your earned income is higher than the basic standard deduction amount.
Given the new senior bonus deduction, the existing extra standard deduction for those over age 65, and changes to the base standard deduction, the highest possible 2027 standard deduction amount is a whopping $48,600.
That amount is for married couples filing jointly who are both age 65 or older, qualify for the bonus deduction, and can claim the extra standard deduction for both spouses.
For more information on how to calculate your total standard deduction, see: The Extra Standard Deduction for People Age 65 and Older .

articles.title_orig: 2 arrested after mushroom gummies given to children on Halloween in Ocean Beach
articles.title_zh: 2 arrested after mushroom gummies given to children on Halloween in Ocean Beach
articles.content_orig:
An 80-year-old man and a 45-year-old man suspected of distributing psilocybin gummies to at least 15 trick-or-treating children in Sunset Cliffs were arrested.
An 80-year-old man and a 45-year-old man suspected of distributing psilocybin gummies, also known as "magic mushrooms" to at least 15 trick-or-treating children in Ocean Beach were taken into custody Wednesday after a a search warrant was served on the home suspected of distributing the psychedelics.
Michael Goff, 80, and Shawn Michael Foster were arrested and booked into the San Diego County Jail. Goff was booked on suspicion of possessing a firearm as a convicted felon, while Foster faces suspicion of possessing both a firearm and ammunition as a convicted felon.
Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7.
No charges were filed in connection with psilocybin-infused gummies but San Diego police said officers discovered an identical bag of psilocybin gummies to those distributed on Halloween in the home during a Wednesday morning search of the home on 2100 block of Sunset Cliffs Boulevard.
Multiple bags of psilocybin-infused gummies were left on a residence's porch Saturday night and were later taken by children between 1 and 6 years old, according to the San Diego Police Department.
Police said the children's parents noticed the suspicious candy packages and, upon inspecting them, suspected they contained controlled substances.
Frank Cary and Cameron Hunter were trick-or-treating with their children and several neighborhood families Saturday night when they made the discovery their children had obtained illicit drugs .
The parents said they were walking just a few yards behind their children when the kids approached a porch with a bowl of what appeared to be candy.
"My 2-year-old went up and grabbed one and started walking away with it in his hand,” Cary told NBC 7. “I noticed the picture had a giraffe and words that looked like they were melting. I took it out of his hand and saw that there was a dosage on the front of it. Five grams, [then I ] flipped it around and read 'psilocybin mushrooms.'”
The parents then confronted the homeowners and later filed a police report with the department, saving the packages of the gummies for law enforcement evaluation, which later tested positive for psilocybin.
NBC 7 San Diego visited the house on Monday and spoke to a man who claimed he lived at the house . The man,  who identified himself as Shawn Barger, disputed the parents' account of the situation. He said his wife had been confused when strangers came to their door and confronted her about the packages.
After the search warrant was served, detectives seized over 2.5 pounds of cannabis, more than 25 grams of crystal methamphetamine, a working digital scale, packaging materials and drug sales ledgers.
An illegally possessed rifle was also located at the residence, along with dozens of rounds of unfired ammunition and a partially assembled pistol.
According to police, a San Diego code compliance investigator responded to the scene to begin a separate investigation into the property's unpermitted living structures.
Anyone with information about the case was urged to contact the Narcotics Unit at 619-531-2468. Tipsters who prefer to remain anonymous can call Crime Stoppers at 888-580-8477.
City News Service contributed to this report.

COLLEGE PARK, Md. – November 5, 2026 – IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.
“I am pleased to report that IonQ delivered its sixth consecutive quarter of record results and the strongest quarter in our company's history,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO. “Third quarter revenue of $173.8 million reflects increasing demand for our quantum technologies and the benefits of our vertically integrated quantum manufacturing capabilities through SkyWater.”
de Masi continued, “Recent developments have provided meaningful validation of our technology and commercial strategy. We are deeply proud that IonQ is the only trapped-ion company to advance to DARPA Stage C. This final stage of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative includes a potential program value of up to $300 million. In addition, NVIDIA will deploy a Superion 256 system as the first on-premise quantum computer at its Accelerated Quantum Research Center – connected directly to its AI supercomputing infrastructure. Both decisions underscore IonQ’s relentless focus on leading the industry with deployable quantum computers – built for data centers and designed to work with classical computing.”
de Masi concluded, “IonQ is building the quantum ecosystem as the first vertically integrated quantum technology company that spans computing, networking, sensing, and security. At SkyWater, we were pleased to welcome Qolab, founded by Nobel Prize winner John Martinis, as a new quantum customer. We also extended our multi-year collaboration with D-Wave and launched our OnRamp Foundry Initiative to accelerate quantum startups from laboratory prototype to commercial manufacturing.”
“One of our customers’ most urgent needs today is cybersecurity that protects them now and keeps them protected as post-quantum standards evolve. Our acquisition of Elisity extends our strategy to meet that need, adding Zero Trust technology that is both a perfect complement and accelerant to our PQC and QKD solutions. We are focused on integrating and leveraging IonQ’s differentiated solutions to drive durable growth and long-term profitability.”
Third Quarter and Recent Commercial Highlights IonQ Platform
“I am thrilled that we continued our growth trajectory in the third quarter, with revenue up 336% year-on-year. Major drivers included global deployments of our IonQ Tempo quantum computers, deliveries of our quantum sensing and space-based solutions, and closing on our acquisition of SkyWater, which had a very strong quarter of its own,” said Inder Singh, COO and CFO. “Our Remaining Performance Obligations more than doubled to $1.2 billion, even as we converted our backlog into record third quarter revenues. This was an especially strong quarter in quantum computing, which represented approximately two-thirds of new contract dollars signed by our IonQ Platform segment, driven by Superion 256 demand. We are pleased to raise our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to an industry record of more than half a billion dollars.”
Singh continued, “IonQ’s strong balance sheet, including $3.7 billion in cash and equivalents pro forma with our recent equity offering, gives us incredible financial firepower to continue investing in our technology, manufacturing infrastructure, and commercial capabilities as we scale the business and capitalize on the growing demand for quantum solutions.”
