Non-GAAP Financial Measures
To supplement IonQ’s condensed consolidated financial statements presented in accordance with GAAP, IonQ uses non-GAAP measures of certain components of financial performance. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EPS are financial measures that are not required by or presented in accordance with GAAP. Management believes that these measures provide investors additional meaningful methods to evaluate certain aspects of the Company’s results period over period.
Adjusted EBITDA is defined as net income (loss) attributable to IonQ, Inc. before net income (loss) attributable to noncontrolling interests, interest income, interest expense, income tax (benefit) expense, depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation, executive cash-based severance, changes in fair value from recurring fair value measurements (such as warrant liabilities, contingent consideration, and investments), offering costs associated with warrants, acquisition transaction and integration costs, and non-cash legal settlements and related costs. Adjusted EPS is defined as net income (loss) per share attributable to IonQ, or EPS, excluding the impact of stock-based compensation, executive cash-based severance, changes in fair value from recurring fair value measurements (such as of warrant liabilities, contingent consideration, and investments), offering costs associated with warrants, acquisition transaction and integration costs, and non-cash legal settlements and related costs. IonQ uses Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EPS to measure the operating performance of its business, excluding specifically identified items that it does not believe directly reflect its core operations and that may not be indicative of recurring operations.
The presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures is not meant to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP, and IonQ’s non-GAAP measures may be different from non-GAAP measures used by other companies. Commercial revenue includes all enterprise agreements with non-U.S. government customers, including agreements with leading universities.

Remaining performance obligations (RPOs) represent the total transaction price from signed contracts that has been allocated to performance obligations that are unsatisfied (or partially unsatisfied) as of the end of the reporting period. articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump .
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war . It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
Aidan  Stretch contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Novartis cites cases of previously unknown tumors possibly tied to its SMA gene therapy
articles.title_zh: Novartis cites cases of previously unknown tumors possibly tied to its SMA gene therapy
articles.content_orig:
By Ed Silverman and Jason Mast
Ed’s stories explore prescription drug pricing, affordability and access, as well issues surrounding patents, litigation, and legislation. He is also the author of the morning Pharmalittle newsletter and the afternoon Pharmalot newsletter .
Jason is a general assignment reporter, with particular focus on genetic medicine and rare disease. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at JasonMast.77.
Novartis has acknowledged seven previously unknown instances in which tumors were found in children who were treated with its spinal muscular atrophy therapy, a surprising development that has raised concerns among families, physicians, and patient advocacy groups.
The cases, which for the moment are being seen as only a potential safety signal, were publicized on Thursday by an advocacy group and on a Facebook page after Novartis earlier this week disclosed the information to neurologists. One advocacy group, SMA Europe, issued a statement saying that regulatory authorities are now examining the cases.
The drugmaker issued its own statement saying that since its treatment — called Zolgensma — was approved in 2019, it has received nine reports of tumors in previously treated patients. Of those, two cases to date showed evidence that the tumors may be linked to the treatment itself.

articles.title_orig: China’s Military Helicopters: A Guide
articles.title_zh: China’s Military Helicopters: A Guide
articles.content_orig:
China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) operates an increasingly diverse fleet of helicopters spanning everything from basic pilot training and battlefield transport to airborne early warning, anti-submarine warfare, and dedicated attack missions.
The force reflects decades of development, often beginning with helicopters acquired from France and later produced under license, before transitioning to increasingly indigenous designs. The result is a mix of older aircraft that have undergone extensive modernization and newer platforms designed around the requirements of China’s expanding military, including its growing carrier and amphibious assault fleets .
The Z-8 family, originally derived from the Cold War-era French Super Frelon , is a particularly good example of this evolution. It has spawned a wide range of specialized variants, including search and rescue, transport, electronic warfare, and airborne command post helicopters. Meanwhile, the Z-20 — frequently alluded to as a Sikorsky S-70/H-60 clone — has emerged as a modern medium-lift platform with land-based, naval, and assault variants, while the Z-10 and newer Z-21 represent China’s growing emphasis on dedicated attack helicopters.
This guide examines the principal helicopter types operated by the PLA, their development, and the roles they are expected to perform.
At the same time, it should be noted that, as it now stands, the PLA remains heavily reliant on foreign-sourced helicopters for a wide variety of applications.
Russian-built helicopters give the PLA a mix of transport and specialized naval capabilities. The Mi-17/171 Hip family supports troop and cargo movement, search and rescue, special operations, and select high-altitude or mission-specific roles. At sea, the Ka-28 Helix provides anti-submarine warfare, while the Ka-31’s radar supports airborne fleet surveillance. These aircraft remain in service where their established capabilities continue to meet operational needs. However, they are increasingly supplemented by Chinese designs, including certain designs that have been tailored to provide direct replacements.
The HC-120 is a light utility helicopter derived from the EC120, a design co-developed by China, France, and Singapore during the 1990s. The type entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2005, providing a modern platform for primary helicopter training and replacing the aging SA316 Alouette III in that role.
The HC-120 is powered by a single Turbomeca Arrius 2F turboshaft engine. Its introduction represented an important step in modernizing the Army Aviation training fleet, giving pilots experience with a more contemporary helicopter before transitioning to larger operational types.
The Z-11 is a light utility helicopter developed by Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation (CHAIC) and the 602 Research Institute. The design is based on the French AS350BA Écureuil , examples of which were acquired for Army Aviation.
Deliveries of the Z-11 to Army Aviation began in 1998. The helicopter is powered by a single WZ-8D turboshaft engine and is primarily used for training, liaison, and other light utility duties.
A scout and armed reconnaissance derivative, designated as the Z-11WB, was developed with a nose-mounted electro-optical (EO) turret and external weapon pylons capable of carrying rockets, missiles, and gun pods. Its operational status remains unclear, although it provided the basis for the unarmed Z-11A training helicopter used by the Army Aviation Academy.
The Z-8 was developed from the French SA321Ja Super Frelon, 13 examples of which China purchased during the late 1970s. Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation subsequently developed an indigenous version during the 1980s.
Powered by three WZ-6 turboshaft engines, the original Z-8 became the foundation for a broad family of helicopters serving the PLA Navy (PLAN), Army Aviation, and People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF).
The Z-8J is the naval transport variant, with a boat-like hull. For anti-submarine warfare (ASW) missions, the helicopter can be equipped with a surface-search radar, a French HS-12 dipping sonar, and Whitehead A244S or ET52 torpedoes.
Several specialized derivatives were developed from the Z-8J:
The Z-8J and Z-8JH have both been used aboard Chinese aircraft carriers, providing transport and support capabilities for embarked naval forces.
The Z-8C represents a substantially improved successor to the original naval Z-8J series. The helicopter was first reported in 2016 and incorporates a number of changes intended to improve its performance and operational versatility.
The most visible differences include a redesigned nose with a chin-mounted weather radar, a FLIR turret, and a pilot night-vision system (PNVS) mounted above the cockpit. A searchlight is also fitted, while the longer engine compartment accommodates the WZ-6C turboshaft engine.
The Z-8C is operated by the PLA Marine Corps, while the Z-8CJ serves as a training variant with the Naval Aviation University.
The helicopter has become a principal transport platform for the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, supporting the movement of troops and equipment between ships and shore.
The PLAAF introduced the Z-8K in 2007 as a dedicated search-and-rescue helicopter. The related Z-8KA is configured for combat search and rescue (CSAR), including the recovery of personnel from hostile or contested environments.
Both versions feature a FLIR turret, searchlight, radar-warning receiver (RWR), chaff and flare dispensers, and a rescue hoist. Some aircraft are also equipped with small terrain-following radars beneath the nose to support low-level operations.
Selected helicopters have received satellite communications (SATCOM) antennas on top of the tail boom, improving their communications capabilities over longer distances.
A further derivative, the Z-8KH, was developed for the PLAAF garrison stationed in Hong Kong. This version is distinguished by chaff and flare dispensers integrated into its flotation equipment.
The Z-8B entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2011 as an improved transport helicopter. It shares several characteristics with the Z-8KH but lacks the latter’s flotation equipment.
The Z-8B incorporates a glass cockpit and has become a major component of the Army Aviation transport fleet. Some aircraft have subsequently had flotation equipment reinstalled, reflecting the type’s continuing evolution.
An optional auxiliary fuel tank can be installed inside the cabin to extend its range. Other upgrades have included SATCOM antennas on the tail boom and, on some aircraft, WZ-6C engines, an EO turret, and a terrain-following radar beneath the nose.
A specialized operations variant has also been identified. These helicopters incorporate RWR, laser-warning receivers (LWR), and missile-approach warning system (MAWS) sensors, alongside flare dispensers and ceramic armor protection.
Lacking the boat-like hull of the Z-8B, the Z-8G is expected to replace that type in Army Aviation service. The helicopter was evaluated from 2014 and was specifically optimized for operations at high altitudes, including in Tibet.
Unlike earlier Z-8 variants, the initial Z-8G configuration uses imported Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-67A turboshaft engines. Its redesigned nose is longer and more aerodynamically efficient, while the glass cockpit and terrain-following radar support operations in demanding environments.
The helicopter also incorporates SATCOM and BeiDou/GPS antennas to improve communications and navigation during long-range missions.
Some Z-8Gs have been equipped for special operations, with combinations of MAWS, RWR, and LWR sensors mounted on the rear fuselage and sponsons, together with chaff and flare dispensers. Armor plates beneath the cockpit windows provide additional protection, and some aircraft carry a 12.7mm machine gun inside a cabin doorway.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low and didn't take into account the company's long-term earnings potential under its new CEO.
The Dublin, Ohio-based burger chain also said Thursday that its board had adopted a “poison pill” plan designed to make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results. Wright, who is the fourth CEO to lead Wendy's since 2024, was previously the president and CEO of Potbelly. He has also held senior leadership roles at Wendy's, Checkers and Domino's Pizza.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose less than 1% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance in the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's shareholder rights plan — commonly known as a “poison pill" plan — grants all shareholders except a hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares and dilute the hostile bidder's ownership stake. It is automatically triggered if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said.
Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. Peltz served as chairman of Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024. His son Bradley Peltz still serves on the company's board and is a Wendy's franchisee.
Dine Brands, the parent company of Applebee's and IHOP, adopted a similar one-year poison pill plan last week to fend off a takeover bid by two investment firms.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy’s is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.
The industry has also been seeing lower U.S. traffic, especially from lower-income customers, as high gas prices and affordability concerns eat into household budgets. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Under Wright, Wendy's has launched a turnaround plan dubbed Dave's Way, which calls for improving food quality, more distinctive marketing and improved digital ordering and restaurant operations.
Wright said Thursday that Wendy's has begun testing quality improvements, including thicker and crispier bacon, creamier Frosties and whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches. The company is removing lower-volume items from its menus to reduce complexity in its kitchens and making breakfast optional, allowing franchisees to focus on their most profitable times of day.
Wendy's on Thursday reported revenue of $547 million in the July-September period. That was better than the $531 million Wall Street had forecast, according to analysts polled by FactSet. Wendy's same-store sales, or sales at locations open at least a year, fell 5.2%, which was also better than the 6.4% drop analysts forecast.
Wendy’s had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 27 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 27 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due to a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

Kyiv’s airstrikes have knocked 15 of Russia’s 38 major oil refineries out of operation — causing more than $23.2 billion in economic damage, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said Thursday.
Just 12 refineries are running at reduced capacity following the precision strikes, which wiped out nearly all of Moscow’s oil sector income from 2025, the HUR estimated.
The agency specifically cited five facilities that were hit as of September, including the massive  Ryazan Oil Refining Company, with those refineries accounting for 33% of Russia’s total volumes.
The strikes have effectively cut Russia’s processing volumes by 55.4% compared to the beginning of the year, Kyiv added.
The attacks have served as a major headache for Moscow, which relies on its oil to fund its ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
The refinery attacks have also led to a gas shortage in various Russian regions, including the annexed Crimea, with more citizens feeling the pain in their wallets over the ongoing war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has reiterated that he would be open to stopping the repeated strikes on Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin halts its attacks on Kyiv’s energy infrastructure.
Moscow has refused to comply , with Zelensky telling world leaders on Thursday that Russian suicide drones continue to hit his country’s critical infrastructure.
“Russians are using Shahed drones and missiles to hit even the energy equipment that our nuclear power plants depend on,” Zelensky said in his address at the Ibero-American Summit. “Every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by Russian attacks.”
Ukraine and Russia continue to trade attacks, with Moscow bombing a postal logistics hub of Nova Poshta, Ukraine’s largest private delivery company, according to the Kremlin.
The Russians also hit a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk and a cargo ship in the Black Sea, the Kremlin said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone strikes set off fires in an industrial zone in the city of Ryazan, about 125 miles southeast of Moscow.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.
The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close.
Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world.
Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.
Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races .
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop."
Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.
Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.
SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings .
Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.
Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia.
Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first.
SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
articles.title_zh: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
articles.content_orig:
Put Muse Realtime Avatar next to HeyGen Video 1 and the first thing that happens is a category error, because only one of them is a model you can invoke. HeyGen Video 1 — the model HeyGen's documentation calls by the identifier heygen-video-1 — is a prompt-to-video generator on POST /v3/models/videos, billed per second of output, live since 30 September 2026. Muse Realtime Avatar is Meta's embodiment layer, rolled out inside the Muse app in the United States on 5 November 2026, with no endpoint, no rate card and no developer documentation at all. One is a line item on an invoice. The other is a feature inside a $20-a-month subscription. The base model and the post-train can be put behind one OpenAI-compatible key instead of two contracts with two vendors.
That does not make the comparison useless. It makes it a comparison of two different purchasing decisions, and the useful version of this page is the one that tells you which decision you are actually making before you spend an afternoon benchmarking the wrong thing.
HeyGen Video 1 answers the question "what should this shot look like?" You give it a prompt, or a prompt and a first frame, or a prompt plus up to nine reference images, three reference videos and three reference audio clips, and it invents the scene — subject, setting, light and sound — in one call. The output is a file. When it finishes, the job is done and you have an MP4.
Muse Realtime Avatar answers a different question: "what should this character's face do while it talks?" It does not decide what to say, and it does not generate a scene from a description. It consumes the speech-token stream produced by Muse Realtime Voice — Meta calls the tokens VQs, and they carry both what is said and how it is delivered — and renders the matching performance in continuous video for as long as the conversation lasts. The output is not a file. It is a live stream that ends when the call ends.
Everything downstream follows from that. HeyGen Video 1 is asynchronous, repeatable and seedable: hold the seed, change one clause, and you get a controlled variation. Muse Realtime Avatar is synchronous, unrepeatable, and has no seed because there is nothing to replay — the same conversation held twice produces two different performances.
Here is the contrast on the six things that actually decide a purchase. Every Muse figure is Meta's own, reported in its 23 September research post; every HeyGen figure is from HeyGen's own documentation or launch material. Neither set has been independently reproduced.
• What it outputs — Muse Realtime Avatar streams a live talking performance of a supplied character; HeyGen Video 1 returns a rendered clip file, MP4/H.264 at 24 fps with 32 kHz stereo AAC audio.
• Frame and resolution — Muse renders 448×768 portrait at 25 fps, a phone-shaped frame; HeyGen Video 1 offers 480p, 768p, 1080p and 2k across six aspect ratios, with 768p as the default.
• Clip length — Muse has no clip; it runs for the length of the conversation. HeyGen Video 1 runs 5 to 30 seconds for text-to-video and image-to-video, and 5 to 15 seconds for reference-to-video or the ultraquality enhancement setting.
• Latency — Muse reports approximately 870 ms from the end of a user's turn to the first byte of synchronized voice and video; HeyGen Video 1 is a batch job, and HeyGen reports 3.7 seconds of diffusion inference for a ten-second image-to-video clip.
• Access — Muse is a consumer feature in the Muse app, US, 18+, with no public API; HeyGen Video 1 is an API-first product with an x-api-key header, an idempotency key, webhooks and signed download URLs.
• Price — Muse has no published price for the avatar and is bundled inside Muse subscriptions at $20 or $100 a month; HeyGen Video 1 is billed per second of generated output, with 1080p and 2k billed at three times the 768p rate.
Both sides publish a speed figure, and putting them next to each other is the most common mistake this comparison invites. Muse's 870 ms and HeyGen's 3.7 seconds measure different things at different scales, and neither is a "time to video."
Meta's 870 ms is a response-start latency inside a live call. It is the gap between you finishing a sentence and the first byte of the reply arriving, and Meta is explicit that it is measured to first byte — not to a complete answer, and not to the tenth minute of a conversation. A system can hit 870 ms and still feel sluggish later, because the interesting property of a causally-generated stream is whether it stays coherent, not whether it starts quickly.
HeyGen's 3.7 seconds is throughput on a batch job: how long the diffusion pass takes to produce a ten-second clip. That is faster than real time in the sense that matters for batch work — you get ten seconds of footage in under four — and it says nothing about interactivity, because there is no interaction to be responsive to.
The comparison that would be fair is Muse's first-byte figure against HeyGen's real-time avatar product, LiveAvatar, which HeyGen advertises with first frames "under 300ms." But LiveAvatar is not HeyGen Video 1 — it is a separate rendering engine on a separate product line, animating a look you already own from a script you already wrote. Meta's own evaluation in September compared Muse Realtime Avatar against LiveAvatar and against Runway Characters, not against a prompt-to-video model, which is a quiet admission that these are different categories.
HeyGen Video 1 has a computable price. Meta's avatar does not, and that asymmetry is more consequential than any spec on this page.
HeyGen launched on 30 September at $0.01 per second of output through October, described in its own copy as 50% off a standard $0.02. The cost chart on the same launch page listed $0.03 as the list price at 768p with audio, a 50% disagreement with its own prose that HeyGen has not resolved. That promotional window has now closed, and the current pricing page sells credits rather than per-second rates — Creator at $29 a month for 600 credits, with HeyGen Video 1 listed as an included capability — so the per-second number a buyer can actually plan against is somewhere between $0.02 and $0.03 at 768p, with 1080p and 2k at three times that.
At the low end, a thousand seconds of 768p output is $20. At the high end it is $30. A thousand seconds at 2k is $60 to $90. Those are real numbers a team can put in a budget, and they buy a specific, repeatable asset: a hundred ten-second clips, or thirty-three thirty-second ones.
Now the same exercise for Muse Realtime Avatar, and it fails immediately. There is no per-second rate because there is no billing unit. Meta sells Muse in token allowances — 500 million Muse tokens a week on the $20 Power plan, 3 billion on the $100 Maximum plan — and has published no conversion between tokens and seconds of rendered avatar video. Anyone who quotes you a per-minute cost for Muse Realtime Avatar is inventing it. The honest statement is that the avatar's marginal cost is unknown even to the person paying the subscription.
What that means in practice depends entirely on which side of the fence you are on. A marketing team producing thirty ad variants a month is buying HeyGen Video 1's per-second arithmetic and getting a predictable bill. A consumer who already pays for Muse is getting the avatar for free at the margin and cannot tell you what it would cost if Meta started charging for it.
It is worth saying plainly, because the framing of a "vs" page usually pushes toward a winner: for most production work, HeyGen Video 1 is the only one of these two you can actually use today.
It gives you resolution above 768p. It gives you six aspect ratios including 21:9 and 9:16. It gives you a seed, so a shot is repeatable, and an idempotency key, so a retry does not double-bill. It gives you a strict schema that rejects unknown fields instead of silently ignoring them, signed download URLs that refresh on poll, and failure codes that distinguish a generation failure from a c

articles.title_zh: Travelers busted at airport with over 3,000 tarantulas hidden away in their socks
articles.content_orig:
Forget snakes on a plane — Peru’s got spiders in socks.
Airport workers in Callao, Peru seized more than 3,000 tarantulas found stuffed inside socks in travelers’ luggage Tuesday.
The employees made the skin-crawling discovery inside the suitcases of three passengers at Jorge Chavez International Airport after recieving an anonymous tip.
The thousands of creepy crawlies were hidden inside 15 to 20 socks in each of the three travelers’ bags and included tarantulas in various stages of development, from eggs to young spiders to fully grown adults.
Officials believe the trio — two Germans and a Pole — planned to smuggle the eight-legged contraband to Germany to sell to arachnid lovers, according to SERFOR, Peru’s National Forestry and Wildlife Service.
Cora Suarez, a wildlife forestry control technician with SERFOR, explained that the hairy, venomous critters can be considered valuable.
“These species are attractive because of the colors, because of the size and, more than anything, because they can be intended for collectors,” Suarez said in Spanish.
All three passengers were detained by Peru’s environmental crimes police and now face prosecution by a specialized environmental prosecutor’s office.
Tuesday’s spider incident is not the first time a multi-legged stowaway has been the victim of an attempted smuggling on board a flight.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
In 2025, more than three dozen live beetles hidden in Japanese snacks were intercepted before they could be smuggled into the US.
Thirty-seven insects were discovered inside potato chips, chocolates and other snacks during a search as the air-cargo shipment arrived at Los Angeles International Airport from Japan, according to US Customs and Border Protection.
The agency noted that the insects are sought after by collectors and are likely worth around $1,500.

articles.title_orig: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.title_zh: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.content_orig:
The four-week average of initial applications for unemployment insurance benefits fell to 194,700, the lowest since 1969, according to the Labor Department today. For just the week through Saturday, initial applications for unemployment benefits fell to 189,000, same as in mid-July, and both were the lowest since 1969.
But the population, the labor force, and employment are vastly bigger now than in the 1960s. So these initial applications, historically low in absolute terms, are amazingly low in relative terms.
The four-week average irons out the week-to-week volatility caused by some states missing the reporting deadline, with those weekly claims then falling into the following week. The purple columns indicate recessions, and what happens to initial claims for unemployment benefits before and during recessions.
There have been waves of layoffs at some companies through the left door, while they hired through the right door – big tech has been doing that now since 2022. Overall, private-sector companies have added to their payrolls at a lethargic pace, with some sectors experiencing labor shortages and hiring booms, and other sectors (such as mortgage lending in 2022 and 2023 and some corners of tech) having experienced substantial payroll reductions. Where Are the Jobs? Winners and Losers by Industry .
In addition, the federal government has shed 328,000 workers since January 2025, and state governments (mostly higher education) have shed 53,000 workers since January 2025.
Laid-off staff who receive severance packages, such as continued salaries for x number of months, cannot file for unemployment benefits since they’re still getting paid by their former employer. Many of them find new jobs within the severance period, collect severance plus the salary at the new job, and so they cannot claim unemployment benefits and don’t show up on the unemployment rolls.
But people who could not find a new job within the severance period are eligible to file for unemployment benefits when the severance expires. Their initial applications for unemployment benefits show up here in the data.
Laid-off H-1B visa holders are generally not eligible to file for unemployment insurance benefits and don’t show up in the data here.
What we’re seeing here is that the crackdown on illegal immigration and on abuses of legal immigration rules has changed the labor market by reducing the supply of labor over the past 18 months, and confirms what the separate data in the monthly employment report has also shown from a different angle.
This declining labor force has kept the labor market relatively tight.
Normally , that combination of big job losses at the federal and state governments, and lethargic payroll increases in the private sector, amid a normally growing labor force, would have led to surging claims for unemployment insurance, and by extension surging unemployment rates (data in the jobs report, the next one tomorrow).
The fact that this hasn’t happened shows the impact of the crackdown on illegal immigration which has caused the labor force to decline this year.
Continued weekly claims for unemployment insurance benefits reflect the total number of people who’d initially applied for unemployment insurance at least a week earlier and who still haven’t found a job and are still claiming unemployment benefits.
Continued claims ticked up to 1.72 million in the latest reporting week, with the four-week average at 1.71 million. The only periods since the 1960s when continued claims were lower were some weeks in 2018-2019 and during the labor shortages after Covid.
With initial claims being very low — meaning, the influx into continued claims is very low — rising or falling continued claims suggest the direction of how long it takes overall for laid-off people to get a new job after claiming unemployment insurance.
When it takes longer overall for them to find a new job and they spend more time on the unemployment insurance rolls, these continued claims rise, and they did that coming out of the labor shortages – but remained historically low.
For the past 12 months, the trend has turned the other way, with people spending less time unemployed before they find a new job, and the number of continued claims has declined since late 2025.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_zh: Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
articles.content_orig:
The shootings took place in rural areas northeast of the city of Afyonkarahisar (pictured)
Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in EskiÅehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.
Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.
In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

articles.title_orig: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.title_zh: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A San Diego-based franchisee of Outback Steakhouse filed for bankruptcy on Monday, citing expensive food and labor costs and declining customer traffic.
Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, which operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations mostly in California, said it has been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic . The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Wilmington, Del., seeking relief from hundreds of millions in debt.
Cerca Trova also operates Outback Steakhouses in Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico but said that California’s minimum wage laws have made labor especially pricey for a majority of its restaurants.
More than half the company’s employees work in California, according to court documents.
California’s minimum wage, effective at the start of this year, is $16.90 per hour. Fast-food employers must pay a higher minimum wage of $20 per hour, but Outback Steakhouse is not classified as a fast-food establishment under the law.
Beverly Hills-based Fat Brands Inc. said in a statement that it filed for bankruptcy on Monday to restructure the debt it accumulated while expanding its company portfolio, citing ‘difficult and largely unforeseen’ market conditions.
“By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged,” Cerca Trova Chief Executive David Goronkin said in a court filing. “Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise.”
The company’s debt has increased from $269 million in late 2020 to $449 million this year. It has between one and 49 creditors, court documents said.
Outback Steakhouse is not the only full-service casual dining restaurant to face challenges since the pandemic.
Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy in 2024, after its disastrous $20 all-you-can-eat shrimp deal . More recently, the Oprah-backed chain True Food Kitchen filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and closed three Southern California locations.
Inflation and economic pressure have led more Americans to eat at home or turn to fast food for a cheaper option, while the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic has curbed customers’ appetites.
The cost of beef has also been rising, up as much as 5% each year since 2022, Cerca Trova said in court filings.
Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Cerca Trova was once the largest Outback Steakhouse franchisee, with 99 restaurants in 2018. As of June, there were 659 Outback Steakhouse locations nationwide, 544 owned and operated by the brand owner, Bloomin’ Brands. The rest are run by franchisees.
Bloomin’ Brands, headquartered in Tampa, Fla., also owns Bonefish Grill, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse and Wine Bar.
The company has thrived this year despite pressures on the restaurant industry, with shares rising 60% since January. Shares fell Tuesday after Cerca Trova’s bankruptcy announcement and ended the day at $10.23, down 6.15%.  The company’s market value is nearly $879 million.
The Scottsdale, Ariz.-based health food chain True Food Kitchen announced it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Monday and has closed 12 locations.
Cerca Trova, also known as Out West Restaurant Group, proposed selling its assets to Bloomin’ Brands for $26.3 million unless a higher offer emerges during the bankruptcy process.
“This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee and does not affect Bloomin’ Brands’ corporate operations, financing, or liquidity,” Bloomin’ Brands spokesperson Elizabeth Daly said in an email. “Bloomin’ Brands is participating in the process as a stalking‑horse bidder to acquire Out West’s assets and seeking to support operational continuity and protect the brand while the court‑supervised process moves forward. ”
Cerca Trova could not be immediately reached for comment.

articles.title_orig: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.title_zh: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.content_orig:
The two companies helmed by the world's richest person have had a rough two-day stretch on the market. Tesla ( TSLA -10.77% ) closed at $398.50 on Election Day, and by 3:08 p.m. ET Thursday, it was trading at about $342, down 14%, representing a loss of about $225 billion in market value. SpaceX ( SPCX -9.05% ) fell from $141.31 to about $125, down 12%, or about $227 billion. Together, that's about $450 billion gone in two sessions, most of it on Thursday, when Tesla fell about 11% and SpaceX about 8%.
To illustrate how steep the drop has been, SpaceX is now trading below its $135 IPO price from June.
Image source: Getty Images.
If you had to sum it up in one word: politics. Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, and Musk, a top ally of President Donald Trump, is a likely target. Speaking on the All-In podcast on election night, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said Democrats had signaled they would use subpoenas "to go after Elon Musk." In Texas, home to both companies, voters elected a Democratic attorney general for the first time since 1994.
But political sentiment isn't the only reason. The Nasdaq was headed for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday as investors dumped chip and data-center stocks, on fears that new leaders in Washington and the states could slow data-center construction. SpaceX, of course, is exposed: Last month, it committed to a roughly $40 billion lease for AI chips with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, with payments starting in the first half of 2027.
Adding to the fire for SpaceX, Wall Street is reportedly trying to sell off pieces of that $40 billion chip deal to other investors, with Goldman Sachs and Apollo leading the effort, according to Bloomberg on Thursday.
SpaceX made money last quarter: $2.79 billion in operating income and $4.4 billion in net income, though it's still $413 million in the red for the first nine months of the year. Nothing that happened in Washington this week changes its launch business or Starlink.
But the fine print, or at least the filing details, are worth noting. That net income included a $390 million tax benefit and a $561 million unrealized gain on its stake in the Boring Company, Musk's tunneling firm, and two customers made up about half of quarterly revenue. Even after the drop, SpaceX is valued at about $1.7 trillion, roughly 150 times its third-quarter operating income on an annualized basis.
Part of Tesla's bull case rests on robotaxis. On Tesla's October earnings call , CFO Vaibhav Taneja told analysts he expects robotaxis to make a real dent in both sales and profits in 2027, and the firm said the Cybercab was due to launch in Dallas this month. Musk told analysts Tesla will end up doing "a majority of all passenger miles on earth" -- "unless we are stopped by governments."
That caveat matters more this week. Self-driving cars depend on regulators, and Washington just got less friendly to Musk. Taneja also conceded that the robotaxi business hasn't yet reached its cost target of 30 cents per mile.
The two companies are also tied together. Tesla's filing puts its SpaceX stake at $2.87 billion as of Sept. 30, and shows SpaceX with a $729 million balance owed to Tesla, most of it tied to Megapack batteries still on order. Bad news for one tends to hit the other.
Not all at once. The political risk is real, but for now it's mostly talk. The new Congress isn't seated until January, and investigations take time. Meanwhile, a two-day drop of 12% to 14% doesn't make either stock cheap.
If you believe in Musk's long-term plans, this is a reasonable time to start a position slowly. Buy in small pieces over several weeks, and keep it a small part of your portfolio, because these are among the most volatile tech stocks you can own.
If you can only pick one, SpaceX gives you a launch and satellite business that's already earning money, while much of Tesla's value rides on robotaxis that are just getting started. And if headlines out of Washington would keep you up at night, it's fine to wait until the political picture is clearer.

articles.title_orig: Parents Sue Google Over A.I. Safety Risks on School Chromebooks
articles.title_zh: Parents Sue Google Over A.I. Safety Risks on School Chromebooks
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Tech giants Google , Meta Platforms and TikTok have launched legal action against California to block the enforcement of a new state law designed to curb social media addiction in children under 16.
The legislation, titled Assembly Bill 1709, bars platforms from exposing minors to "psychologically exploitative features" that trigger compulsive usage, including algorithmic recommendations and autoplaying video functions. It further mandates the removal of young users' accounts that incorporate such tools.
In distinct lawsuits submitted on Wednesday, the companies claimed the statute unfairly compels them to follow California’s favoured method of displaying content to children, overriding parental control.
The platforms asserted that the law infringes upon First Amendment free speech guarantees within the US Constitution, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which provides broad legal protection to websites regarding user-submitted content.
Responding on Thursday, the office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the sole defendant tasked with enforcing state legislation. said it was reviewing the legal challenges.
"Our office is committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online," the office stated. Google is an Alphabet subsidiary that owns YouTube, Meta operates Facebook and Instagram, and TikTok belongs to Chinese firm ByteDance.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10, saying children's safety ‌should be central to any discussion about technology, and California "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk."
The law takes effect on January 1, 2027, unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold. "Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families," Google ⁠spokesperson Jose Castaneda said on Thursday.
"Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts, while leaving children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services. TikTok, meanwhile, said protected speech "cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable."
Other critics also accused California of overreaching. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law "a massive privacy and free speech nightmare."
Many US states regulate children's access to social media. Countries around the ​world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and limit teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all US states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws. Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in ‌Los Angeles.
The companies and Snapchat parent Snap ​still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and ‌other government entities claiming they sought to addict children ​and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

articles.title_orig: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.title_zh: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Here are the federal income tax brackets for 2027:
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended strikes on Russian oil facilities in an exclusive Fox News interview with Trey Yingst, saying Ukraine's response to Moscow's attacks "must be painful."
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is defying calls from the Trump administration for his armed forces to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, telling Fox News: "Our response must be painful."
In an interview in Kyiv, Zelenskyy acknowledged holding discussions with the Trump administration about targeting oil facilities, attacks President Donald Trump has pinned as being partly to blame for high gas prices in the U.S.
"We had different conversations — different, and several — with President Trump and with his team about attacks on refineries," Zelenskyy said.
"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system."
TRUMP TELLS ZELENSKYY TO STOP DOING 'ONE THING' DURING ATTACKS ON RUSSIA
During an interview with Fox News, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged President Donald Trump to pursue an energy cease-fire with Russia as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. (Fox News)
Ukraine has reported near-daily Russian strikes on energy infrastructure , triggering power outages just as temperatures dip ahead of winter.
"That's why we have to respond. But our response has to be painful for Russian military people," Zelenskyy said. "If we will not respond on energy, they will continue."
U.S.-Ukraine relations took a further hit in October when Trump struck a deal to import millions of tons of Russian diesel to the United States.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
Zelenskyy warned President Donald Trump against helping Russia while praising first lady Melania Trump’s role in securing a humanitarian evacuation from Russian-controlled territory. (Fox News)
Zelenskyy suggested Ukraine might be encouraged to hold off on further attacks on Russian oil facilities if the United States were to deliver more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors to protect Ukrainian skies. Pressed by Fox News on whether that might be seen as an attempt to leverage Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."
"Our countries are huge partners. American society (is a) huge supporter."
"And that's why I have to share with (the) president the truth, the real situation: that America can't help Russia. (The) president can't help Putin ."
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News that Ukraine will continue targeting Russian oil refineries despite objections from the Trump administration. (Pier Marco Tacca; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Ahead of planned peace talks in the United Arab Emirates, Zelenskyy urged Trump to launch another push for a targeted ceasefire where both Russia and Ukraine refrain from attacks on energy facilities.
"If the American president thinks that this war has influence on the prices," Zelenskyy said, "he can ask, energy ceasefire, during (the) Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting: energy ceasefire."
Zelenskyy spoke with Fox News hours before starved and exhausted residents left the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky and crossed into Ukrainian-held territory under a humanitarian truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump , the first of its kind in more than four years of war.

Zelenskyy welcomed the first lady's initiative, calling the evacuations "a huge result," and adding: "I don't know how many such steps will be available for us, but if the first lady can do it ... it's very helpful. I'm very thankful to her."
Trey Yingst currently serves as chief foreign correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in August 2018.

articles.title_orig: McDonald's plans new value menu offerings next year to boost sluggish sales
articles.title_zh: McDonald's plans new value menu offerings next year to boost sluggish sales
articles.content_orig:
A ‘Barron’s Roundtable' panel discusses how the fast-food chain will manage the pinch to consumers wallets.
McDonald's is testing new value menu offerings with an eye toward launching a new national value menu program in early 2027.
The fast-food giant has sought to counter slowing traffic in the U.S. as the company's quarterly earnings release on Wednesday revealed comparable sales in the U.S. declined 0.2% in the third quarter.
McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said during the company's most recent earnings call that, in the last week of October, McDonald's began an eight-week test of two new everyday affordable price menu constructs across all day parts at about 1,900 restaurants in a handful of regions.
The test involves mix-and-match bundles to give customers greater choices that are similar to prior buy one, add one offers, as well as fixed bundles with a set combination.
MCDONALD'S TO SPEND $8.5B ON REVAMPING RESTAURANTS, TECH AND FRANCHISE SUPPORT
The McDonald's CEO added that a group of franchisees representing about 4,000 restaurants are moving forward with similar entry-level bundles in advance of the formal test results. Kempczinski said the two groups together "represent more than 40% of the U.S. system, reflecting strong alignment around the opportunity."
McDonald's is planning to roll out a new value menu push early next year after it assesses the results of tests to close out this year. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"We use the results of this test to determine which structure resonates most with customers, works best operationally and delivers sustainable incremental traffic and sales for franchisees," Kempczinski said. "Our goal is to launch a new program nationally in early 2027.
"Our goal is straightforward. Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald's, whether they're looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal or a digital offer in the mobile app."
MCDONALD'S SAYS US SALES SLOWED AFTER VALUE DEAL PUSH FELL SHORT

The value menu plans come after McDonald's in September announced a multi-year plan called "NEXT" that will focus on upgrading restaurants and staff training, as well as deploying technology.
The company will spend $8.5 billion as part of the NEXT strategy through 2036, with about $5 billion of that spending provided through 2030. The NEXT partnering support for franchisees will include a combination of capital support and rent relief.

McDonald's global CFO Ian Borden said on the earnings call that the fast-food chain is already putting elements of the NEXT strategy into action, including rolling out a new beverage platform , starting the "Make It Golden" training initiative, and setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken.
Borden added that the company is starting to open remodeled NEXT restaurants around the world, including the first international restaurant in Poland.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices hit two-month low following decisive midterm election results
articles.title_zh: Oil prices hit two-month low following decisive midterm election results
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices jumped Thursday, as investors reassessed the outlook for ‌the US-Israeli war with Iran while new attacks on tankers fed worries about oil supplies.
Brent crude futures rose 4% to $98.44 a barrel by 2:42 p.m. ET. US West Texas Intermediate crude increased 2.9% to $90.71 a barrel.
On Wednesday, both benchmarks tumbled more than 8% to their lowest settlement levels since August 31.
"The situation in the Middle East is ​still unresolved and that's why there is some modest recovery in prices at the moment," said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at UBS.
Andy Lipow, ​president of Lipow Oil Associates, said reports of tankers striking mines in the Middle East or being targeted by drones continue ⁠to worry the oil market. Investors are also worried about Iran's unchanged position regarding negotiations with the US.
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are ​still running close to a record pace with at least five vessels having reported incidents since Sunday, according to UK maritime security agency UKMTO. The pace was ​similar to October when the agency said 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war.
The war on Iran, which US President Donald Trump launched along with Israel in February, resulted in sharply higher fuel prices, which became major grievances for voters. Democrats took control of both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, routing Trump's ​Republican Party.
The new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January.
Citi said in a note there were concerns that with the midterms over, the White House could ​focus on its executive powers in foreign policy and potentially escalate the war with Iran.
Eurasia Group, however, lowered its estimate for the chance of renewed US strikes on ‌Iran ⁠to 60% from 65%. It also cut the probability of a deal to 10% from 20%, as Iran has held firm on demands that Trump is viewed as unlikely to accept. Eurasia Group raised the likelihood of a continued standoff to 30% from 15%.
Despite the recent drop in oil prices, any escalation in the conflict could push Brent into a $110 to $125 per barrel range, Eurasia Group said in a note.
Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi discussed the "latest progress" in diplomatic efforts to ​promote regional stability in separate calls ​with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts, the ⁠Iranian foreign ministry said.
Tensions in the region remain elevated. Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the kingdom's Red Sea oil export hub, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis continued attacks on the kingdom ​in another front of the Iran war.
The Houthis later said they attacked King Fahd airport in the Saudi city of Dammam, although ​there was no immediate ⁠confirmation from Saudi authorities.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to use unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Elsewhere, Ukraine renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries, raising concerns about Russia's ability to export diesel under a deal with Trump.
The Ryazan oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, ⁠appeared to ​have been targeted in a large overnight drone attack on industrial sites southeast of Moscow, ​according to a Reuters video analysis.
If confirmed, it would be the second Russian refinery hit this week, following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant on Monday night.
